name: Boethius's philosophic calm amid an age of superstition
plain_explanation: Written by a man awaiting execution, the Consolation shows none of the era's obsession with sin or morbid superstition; instead it displays a serene, rational, almost Socratic composure.
precise_definition: The distinctive tone Russell identifies in the Consolation: 'perfect philosophic calm,' free of the superstition, sin-obsession, and 'excessive straining after the unattainable' typical of the age, more reminiscent of Plato than of Plotinus.
why_it_mattered: It is what makes Boethius, in Russell's judgment, utterly exceptional for his era -- a man free from superstition and fanaticism unmatched, Russell says, in the two centuries before or the ten centuries after him, and not paralleled again until after Newton.
historical_origin: Attributed by Russell partly to Boethius's Roman aristocratic background, which may have made freedom from superstition less exceptional than elsewhere, though its combination with deep learning and public-spiritedness was, Russell says, unique for the age.
examples: The concluding poem on cosmic love and order, which Russell quotes in full and compares to Pope's Essay on Man
influence_on_later_thinkers: Contributed to the Consolation's enormous medieval popularity and its influence on Dante, who Russell notes was likely influenced by its alternation of verse and prose in the Vita Nuova.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Notable for its comparative absence of religious anxiety despite being written by a condemned man under a Christian government.
